items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-10-26
items.q: No, I never knew him. I never met him.

ctx.x: Did you ever see Jelly Roll Martin?

No, I never knew him. I never met him. In fact, I never knew Joe Oliver. I never met Pompous Celestine to La New Orleans Jazz Club down here, and Miss Menville introduced me to him. And she asked him, was this one of the men who used to sit down and listen to you? He said, no, ma'am. I never seen this man in my life before. I had already told her I never met him, but she didn't believe it, but she tried to put me on the spot. But that Negro had more honesty and truthfulness in his body than Miss Menville has in…
Was Celestine playing when you were a young man?

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: The swing pianists were Albert K-A-L, Cal, I suppose that's Carroll, Lewis Wade, Clarence Williams, Tony Jackson, Steve Lewis, and Jelly Roll Morton.

ctx.x: It is an original Negro tune, which was made up down south. It was named Tiger Rag when the Dixieland Band brought it up north. Buddy, you want me to continue with this? Yeah, go on. Buddy Bolden was the hottest cornetist in the world, and he played so much that he is in the insane asylum now if he is still living. After this time came King Oliver, Punk, and Freddie Capron, that's spelled K-E-P-P-E-R-T, and the original Creole Band. They were the last word and swing cornet players. The swing pianists were Albert…

We used to have swing sessions every morning around 3 o'clock after the boys got through with their work and each man would do his bit. Quote, the first hot band to leave from the South and introduce swing music was the Creole Jazz Band, unquote, says Mr. Williams. Quote, following the Dixieland Jazz Band, which recorded Livery Stable Blues and Tiger Ray, which swept the country. The Creole Band was colored and the Dixieland Band was white and they used to play across the street from each other and used to sit in…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-26
items.q: because I never heard him, and I never heard him today.

ctx.x: Wait a minute, I can't hear. No, one Dirt. Tiger Rag. We did go over Tiger Rag a little bit, but...

Well, there we go again. As much has been said about the Tiger Rag, Alan Lomax discovered a man, well, called Jelero Martin. A man who's never been honored or given credit for anything. That he's done anything. Maybe he played good jazz, I don't know. But it would have to be after the original Dixieland jazz band, because I never heard him, and I never heard him today. They discovered this man, and he goes in the archers of the United States government somewhere, where they keep this folk music. Set him up two…

and then different ideas come to you, you try to put them together. My inability to learn new music put me on my own, that I had to make up my own music if I wanted to be different and have them play different tunes or play the same tune all night. Well, now I'm going to take this Tiger Rag apart. The beginning of this Tiger Rag begins with an ending that I always made to my numbers. And this is it. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Now, if anyone has any musical ears at all, they'll hear that in many other endings…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-06-14
items.q: Well, as far as him, he stole his music from the original Dixieland jazz band.

ctx.x: So that the opening words of the late Jelly Roll Morton on his talk for the Library of Congress in Washington, with Alan Lomax, is wrong completely. He says from the very first, the first words he says on those records is, jazz started in New Orleans. And he goes on to tell about how he wrote Tiger Rag, how he named it, and how it was based on the old French quadrilles and all the rest of that stuff. Well, you've told me already, and I believe you absolutely, that that is just so much hooey.
Well, as far as him, he stole his music from the original Dixieland jazz band. You don't have to go any further than that Mellenberg Jaws.
